answer.rationale:
memory_c2 is the load-bearing memory here: it is the only record that would justify moving primary supply to the low-cost vendor, and it is exactly the record the current low-cost quote makes tempting. It is also the weakest fit to today's conditions \u2014 it says 'last year', it reports on cost and invoicing accuracy but is silent on on-time delivery performance, ramp capacity, and behavior under stress, and the one memory that does speak to supply fragility (memory_c3) concerns a shortage the low-cost vendor was never tested against. So I spend the single verification pull on memory_c2 to see whether the original record covered delivery reliability at committed volume or only price and paperwork.

Meanwhile the situation constrains the action independently of what the archive returns. The line is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer and the contract lapses in 14 days without auto-renewal. Deferring is not the low-risk option it was in memory_c5 \u2014 that memory concerned a non-critical month-to-month service, not an expiring primary supply contract, so it does not transfer. A primary-vendor switch inside 14 days with zero buffer puts delivery risk up front to chase a cost target, which directly violates the stated objective; memory_c2's 'onboarding was quick' is not evidence that onboarding is quick at 94% utilization with no slack to absorb a slipped first shipment. Adding a second source (memory_c3) is the right structural move but does not by itself hit the 18% mandate and burns the one decision slot.

Negotiating at renewal is the action that spends the slot best: memory_c4 shows benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and terms, memory_c6 shows multi-year commitment unlocks volume pricing without narrowing scope, and memory_c1 shows renewal preserves integration stability and uninterrupted deliveries. The live low-cost quote is real leverage rather than a plan of record. I intend to negotiate a benchmarked renewal, using the quote as the anchor and a longer term as the price lever, and to keep the second source queued as the next cycle's decision.

Uncertainty I am not resolving: whether negotiation closes the full 18% gap, and whether the low-cost vendor could in fact hold committed volume. If the incumbent will not move far enough, the gap becomes a scoped, buffered qualification of the low-cost vendor next cycle \u2014 not an unhedged switch now. I also flag that hitting 18% purely on unit price risks quality, lead-time, and scope erosion that would not surface until after this review; that cost should be tracked, not assumed away.
